title: Cork
subject: reading

paragraphs.text: Cork - the thick bark of the cork oak tree (Quercus suber) - is a remarkable material. It is tough, elastic, buoyant, and fire-resistant, and suitable for a wide range of purposes. It has also been used for millennia: the ancient Egyptians sealed their sarcophagi (stone coffins) with cork, while the ancient Greeks and Romans used it for anything from beehives to sandals.

And the cork oak itself is an extraordinary tree. Its bark grows up to 20 cm in thickness, insulating the tree like a coat wrapped around the trunk and branches and keeping the inside at a constant 20°C all year round. Developed most probably as a defence against forest fires, the bark of the cork oak has a particular cellular structure - with about 40 million cells per cubic centimetre - that technology has never succeeded in replicating. The cells are filled with air, which is why cork is so buoyant.It also has an elasticity that means you can squash it and watch it spring back to its original size and shape when you release the pressure.

Cork oaks grow in a number of Mediterranean countries, including Portugal, Spain, Italy, Greece and Morocco. They flourish in warm, sunny climates where there is a minimum of 400 millimetres of rain per year, and not more than 800 millimetres. Like grape vines, the trees thrive in poor soil, putting down deep roots in search of moisture and nutrients. Southern Portugal's Alentejo region meets all of these requirements, which explains why, by the early 20th century, this region had become the world's largest producer of cork, and why today it accounts for roughly half of all cork production around the world.

Most cork forests are family-owned. Many of these family businesses, and indeed many of the trees themselves, are around 200 years old. Cork production is, above all, an exercise in patience. From the planting of a cork sapling to the first harvest takes 25 years, and a gap of approximately a decade must separate harvests from an individual tree. And for top-quality cork, it's necessary to wait a further 15 or 20 years. You even have to wait for the right kind of summer's day to harvest cork. If the bark is stripped on a day when it's too cold - or when the air is damp - the tree will be damaged.

Cork harvesting is a very specialised profession. No mechanical means of stripping cork bark has been invented, so the job is done by teams of highly skilled workers. First, they make vertical cuts down the bark using small sharp axes, then lever it away in pieces as large as they can manage. The most skilful cork-strippers prise away a semi-circular husk that runs the length of the trunk from just above ground level to the first branches. It is then dried on the ground for about four months, before being taken to factories, where it is boiled to kill any insects that might remain in the cork. Over 60% of cork then goes on to be made into traditional bottle stoppers, with most of the remainder being used in the construction trade. Corkboard and cork tiles are ideal for thermal and acoustic insulation, while granules of cork are used in the manufacture of concrete.

Recent years have seen the end of the virtual monopoly of cork as the material for bottle stoppers, due to concerns about the effect it may have on the contents of the bottle. This is caused by a chemical compound called 2,4,6-trichloroanisole (TCA), which forms through the interaction of plant phenols, chlorine and mould. The tiniest concentrations - as little as three or four parts to a trillion - can spoil the taste of the product contained in the bottle. The result has been a gradual yet steady move first towards plastic stoppers and, more recently, to aluminium screw caps. These substitutes are cheaper to manufacture and, in the case of screw caps, more convenient for the user.

The classic cork stopper does have several advantages, however. Firstly, its traditional image is more in keeping with that of the type of high quality goods with which it has long been associated. Secondly - and very importantly - cork is a sustainable product that can be recycled without difficulty. Moreover, cork forests are a resource which support local biodiversity, and prevent desertification in the regions where they are planted. So, given the current concerns about environmental issues, the future of this ancient material once again looks promising.

groups.instruction:
Questions 1-5

Choose TRUE if the statement agrees with the information given in the text,

choose FALSE if the statement contradicts the information,

or choose NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

questions.prompt: The cork oak has the thickest bark of any living tree.
questions.explanation:
参考译文: 栓皮栎树拥有所有现在树木中最厚的树皮。

定位词: The cork oak

对应 第一段第一句: Cork - the thick bark of the cork oak tree (Quercus suber) - is a remarkable material.

本题出现了绝对化表达the thickest bark,答题时需要格外关注。根据题目中的cork oak及bark可以定位到文章首段首句，该句说cork是the thick bark of the cork oak tree,并且这是一种remarkable material,在本段后几句中，对cork的特点以及以往用途进行了介绍，但对于“cork oak的bark是不是the thickest”这一问题，完全没有提及，因此本题答案为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: Scientists have developed a synthetic cork with the same cellular structure as natural cork.
questions.explanation:
参考译文: 科学家研发出了人造栓皮,它们与天然栓皮具有同样的细胞结构。

定位词: cellular structure

文中对应点 第二段第三句: Developed most probably as a defense against forest fires, the bark of the cork oak has a particular cellular structure - with about 40 million cells per cubic centimeter - that technology has never succeeded in replicating.

关于栓皮细胞结构的内容出现在第二段第三句，本句说明了栓皮的特殊细胞结构从来没有被技术成功复制过，因此与题目中科学家研发出了人造栓皮，与天然栓皮细胞结构一致的表达相反，因此本题答案为FALSE。

questions.prompt: Individual cork oak trees must be left for 25 years between the first and second harvest.
questions.explanation:
参考译文: 一株栓皮栎树第-一次收获和第二次收获之间必须间隔25年。

定位词: the first and second harvest

文中对应点 第四段第四句: From the planting of a cork sapling to the first harvest takes 25 years,and a gap of approximately a decade must separate harvests from an individual tree.

本题问关于栓皮栎树的成长过程，题目中说第一次收获和第二次收获之间必须间隔25年。而按照原文第四段第四句的表述，从planing of a cork sapling 到first harvest需要25年，之后a gap of approximately a decade must separate harvests from an individual tree,由此可以判断题目中关于栓皮栎树的表述与原文是不一致的，因此本题答案为FALSE。

questions.prompt: Cork bark should be stripped in dry atmospheric conditions.
questions.explanation:
参考译文: 栓皮应该在干燥的空气条件下剥开。

定位词: cork bark, stripped

对应第四段第六、七句: You even have to wait for the right kind of summer's day to harvest cork. If the bark is stripped on a day when it's too cold - or when the air is damp - the tree will be damaged.

关于cork bark在怎样的条件剥皮的表述出现在原文第四段末尾，其中第六、七句说需要在right kind of summer's day进行,如果天气太冷,空气潮湿,树木则会受到破坏，所有本题说在dry atmospheric conditions进行是正确的，因此本题答案为TRUE。

questions.prompt: The only way to remove the bark from cork oak trees is by hand.
questions.explanation:
参考译文: 唯一从栓皮栎树上剥下栓皮的方式是用手进行。

定位词: The only way to remove the bark from cork oak trees

文中对应点 第五段第一、二句: Cork harvesting is a very specialised profession. No mechanical means of stripping cork bark has been invented, so the job is done by teams of highly skilled workers.本题问将树皮从cork oak tree上剥下的方式，原文第五段写道cork harvesting 是非常专业化的职业，人们没有发明出mechanical means,这项工作是由teams of highly skilled workers完成的,这与题目中“只能通过by hand的方式进行”这一表述一致。需要注意的是，题目中出现绝对词only需要格外关注，但不要先人为主地认为在这种情况下题目与原文多数会出现矛盾，因此本题答案为TRUE。

题号：10

定位词：made from

第七段第三句：Secondly - and very importantly - cork is a sustainable product that can be recycled without difficulty.

本题问cork bottle stoppers来自一种怎样的材料，文中第七段第三句说cork是一种sustainable product，与本题的含义一致，因此本题答案为sustainable。

定位词：easily

第七段第三句：Secondly - and very importantly - cork is a sustainable product that can be recycled without difficulty.

第七段第三句提到cork是一种sustainable material，之后进行了解释：that can be recycled without difficulty，此处without difficulty与题目中easily为同义替换，根据题目与原文的对应情况，答案应填入recycled。

题号：12

定位词：aid

第七段第四句：Moreover, cork forests are a resource which support local biodiversity, and prevent desertification in the regions where they are planted.

Cork forests出现在第七段第四句，本句说cork forests可以support local biodiversity，此处support与题目中aid同义替换，本题答案为biodiversity。

题号：13

定位词：stop

第七段第四句：Moreover, cork forests are a resource which support local biodiversity, and prevent desertification in the regions where they are planted.

第七段第四句是关于cork forest的好处，提到support local biodiversity and prevent desertification，其中prevent与题目中stop sth. happening含义一致，因此本题答案为desertification。

articleHtml:
Cork

Cork - the thick bark of the cork oak tree (Quercus suber) - is a remarkable material. It is tough, elastic, buoyant, and fire-resistant, and suitable for a wide range of purposes. It has also been used for millennia: the ancient Egyptians sealed their sarcophagi (stone coffins) with cork, while the ancient Greeks and Romans used it for anything from beehives to sandals.

And the cork oak itself is an extraordinary tree. Its bark grows up to 20 cm in thickness, insulating the tree like a coat wrapped around the trunk and branches and keeping the inside at a constant 20°C all year round. Developed most probably as a defence against forest fires, the bark of the cork oak has a particular cellular structure - with about 40 million cells per cubic centimetre - that technology has never succeeded in replicating. The cells are filled with air, which is why cork is so buoyant.It also has an elasticity that means you can squash it and watch it spring back to its original size and shape when you release the pressure.

Cork oaks grow in a number of Mediterranean countries, including Portugal, Spain, Italy, Greece and Morocco. They flourish in warm, sunny climates where there is a minimum of 400 millimetres of rain per year, and not more than 800 millimetres. Like grape vines, the trees thrive in poor soil, putting down deep roots in search of moisture and nutrients. Southern Portugal's Alentejo region meets all of these requirements, which explains why, by the early 20th century, this region had become the world's largest producer of cork, and why today it accounts for roughly half of all cork production around the world.

Most cork forests are family-owned. Many of these family businesses, and indeed many of the trees themselves, are around 200 years old. Cork production is, above all, an exercise in patience. From the planting of a cork sapling to the first harvest takes 25 years, and a gap of approximately a decade must separate harvests from an individual tree. And for top-quality cork, it's necessary to wait a further 15 or 20 years. You even have to wait for the right kind of summer's day to harvest cork. If the bark is stripped on a day when it's too cold - or when the air is damp - the tree will be damaged.

Cork harvesting is a very specialised profession. No mechanical means of stripping cork bark has been invented, so the job is done by teams of highly skilled workers. First, they make vertical cuts down the bark using small sharp axes, then lever it away in pieces as large as they can manage. The most skilful cork-strippers prise away a semi-circular husk that runs the length of the trunk from just above ground level to the first branches. It is then dried on the ground for about four months, before being taken to factories, where it is boiled to kill any insects that might remain in the cork. Over 60% of cork then goes on to be made into traditional bottle stoppers, with most of the remainder being used in the construction trade. Corkboard and cork tiles are ideal for thermal and acoustic insulation, while granules of cork are used in the manufacture of concrete.

Recent years have seen the end of the virtual monopoly of cork as the material for bottle stoppers, due to concerns about the effect it may have on the contents of the bottle. This is caused by a chemical compound called 2,4,6-trichloroanisole (TCA), which forms through the interaction of plant phenols, chlorine and mould. The tiniest concentrations - as little as three or four parts to a trillion - can spoil the taste of the product contained in the bottle. The result has been a gradual yet steady move first towards plastic stoppers and, more recently, to aluminium screw caps. These substitutes are cheaper to manufacture and, in the case of screw caps, more convenient for the user.

The classic cork stopper does have several advantages, however. Firstly, its traditional image is more in keeping with that of the type of high quality goods with which it has long been associated. Secondly - and very importantly - cork is a sustainable product that can be recycled without difficulty. Moreover, cork forests are a resource which support local biodiversity, and prevent desertification in the regions where they are planted. So, given the current concerns about environmental issues, the future of this ancient material once again looks promising.
